prize_parts.citation: for formalising how organised political interests shape trade policy, and for analysing the interplay of trade, innovation and growth

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B001 with Helpman and Grossman, a single part. After the exchange I still think it is the contribution that best meets the common criteria of a big question, explanatory power, clear attribution and maturity. Grossman and Helpman took a long-standing puzzle, why governments depart from free trade, and turned it into a tractable model in which organised interests bid for policy. That produced a structural empirical literature, even though estimates vary. The same partnership built the models of innovation, trade and growth in open economies. Those connect trade to endogenous growth theory, so the influence is not confined to trade and political economy. This is from recollection and I have not verified it. Attribution is two people with sustained joint work, and every colleague who discussed it described it as the cleanest on the shortlist. Three decades of extension, teaching and critique leave no maturity question. Of the written weaknesses, B001's is a matter of weighting, namely how much a framework's influence should count against mixed confirmation. B020's, as I read it, is a credit boundary that the committee cannot repair by adding names that are not on the credited list. That asymmetry is why I keep B001 first.
statement.case_against: The empirical record is the real weakness. Tests of the protection-for-sale predictions give mixed and specification-dependent results, so the case rests on the framework's influence on how questions are posed and measured, not on settled confirmation. Friberg, Strömberg and Enflo are right that B020 has changed data use and quantitative policy evaluation more visibly, and I take that as a serious reason to rank it above B001. Another reason is that Helpman is credited on both B001 and B020, so recognising him under B001 means choosing one strand of his work. Trade was last recognised in 2008. I treat that as field balance, not merit, and it applies equally to B020. I also do not claim that a framework earns a prize merely because its tests are contested. The committee needs a citation that says plainly what is being credited: the framework and the research it opened, not a confirmed set of predictions.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B020 first and B001 eighth. He argues that the selection and reallocation mechanisms have been checked against firm-level data across many countries and have changed estimation and policy evaluation, whereas the protection-for-sale predictions have not been confirmed as consistently. He would accept B001 only as a second choice.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my configuration. It has narrowed my confidence, but it has not changed my ranking. We agree on the facts. We differ on whether a widely used workhorse for measurement should outrank a framework whose influence runs ahead of its confirmation. I put weight on attribution that is not in dispute. If the Committee chose B020, the Scientific Background would have to explain why Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited, and a citation cannot fix that. For B001 the only open question is the weighting you raise. I accept that reasonable members will weigh these differently. If the Committee prefers B020, I would support it as a single-part award with Helpman credited once, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first. He wants the case to stand on protection for sale and the trade-innovation-growth models rather than on credit Helpman earned elsewhere. He names the mixed empirical record as his main reservation and the B020 credit gap as the reason he ranks B020 below B001.
responses.response: I agree. To be clear about my own position, B001 must not borrow strength from Helpman's firm-heterogeneity work. If it does not stand on its own merits, it should not win. I also agree the empirical limitation should be stated openly in the citation and background. The chair asked what supports impact beyond trade theory and political economy. My answer, from recollection, is that the open-economy growth models feed into endogenous growth theory, and that the lobbying framework gave other fields a template for modelling policy as an outcome of influence. Our difference is smaller than it looks: you would keep B020 as your first alternative, and I am moving B020 to the front of my alternatives.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B020 first and accepts that the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a real risk. He leans towards treating it as not disqualifying but holds that view with moderate confidence. He would recognise Helpman for firm heterogeneity and treat B001 as an alternative, not a second claim.
responses.response: I appreciate that he calls the gap a risk and not a footnote. His view that it is probably not disqualifying is reasonable, but he holds it with moderate confidence and I find that telling. I also agree that the committee should not credit Helpman twice. We come to the same fork from opposite sides. The difference is that he accepts an attribution risk in exchange for the wider empirical footprint, while I accept a thinner empirical record in exchange for clean attribution. I have not found an argument in the exchange that shows his weighting is better than mine, nor the reverse. I think the committee has to settle this by judgement and should not pretend the gap or the mixed tests can be explained away.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B019 first and B001 second. She holds that a framework's influence is stronger when its core claims have been tested directly, and that the China-shock designs have largely held up. She would limit the citation to Autor, Hanson and Dorn on adjustment to trade and technological change.
responses.response: I accept her point that tested and robust designs are valuable, and that is why I keep B019 as an alternative. Her narrower citation is sensible and her argument for Dorn alongside Autor and Hanson is persuasive, since the China-shock papers are a joint body of work. I still have two worries that her reply did not resolve. The magnitude and long-run persistence are still debated. And the task strand overlaps with Acemoglu and Restrepo outside the credited list, which makes B019's attribution question larger than B001's. I rank B019 third overall, behind B020, because of the attribution question, not because I think it is scientifically weaker.

uncertainties: How much the mixed empirical record of protection for sale should count against its conceptual influence; the exchange has clarified this question but not resolved it.
Whether the Committee will treat the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum omission as disqualifying for B020, which is the main thing that would move me towards that candidate.
Whether the open-economy growth models add distinct credit to B001 or overlap with other recognised growth theory; this is from recollection and I have not verified it.
Whether the China-shock and task strands in B019 form one achievement, and whether Dorn or Katz is the right third name.

My assessments of citations and priority come from recollection of the literature and the colleagues' written positions, not independent verification, and I do not treat support counts as scientific merit.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot ID, including B001, B020 and B019. My work on labour economics and crime is adjacent to B019 and B014, but no personal or collaborative connection to those candidates is apparent. I disclose this without adjudicating it.
